In April I decided to share my thoughts with the EPA administrator ahead of their review of air quality standards (NAAQS = National Ambient Air Quality Standards). Unfortunately, the EPA decided to maintain the NAAQS for lead at 0.15 micro grams per cubic meter over a 3-month period.

 

April 5th, 2015

Dear Administrator McCarthy,

 

I am writing to you as a concerned citizen who believes that lead exposure is an important public health concern. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, over half a million young children in the United States have blood lead levels of 5µg/dL or more [0]. To date, there is no accepted threshold below which lead does not cause neurocognitive toxicity [1]. The effects of early childhood lead exposure are not altogether transient; indeed, the EPA’s Integrated Science Assessment for Lead concluded that “the neurotoxic effects of Pb are not generally reversible” [2]. Taken together, these three data points bring me to believe that a socially responsible ambient air quality standard for lead should intend to reduce lead exposure as much as realistically possible. I believe the current NAAQS for lead (0.15 µg/m3 based on a rolling 3-month average) is much too lenient given lead’s unique tendency to persist in the environment and bioaccumulate. A more rigorous standard is realistic and attainable.

 

The national estimate of lead emissions from the consumption of aviation gasoline (avgas) was 483 tons in 2011, according to the EPA’s National Emissions Inventory [3]. Interestingly, of the 73 different facility types catalogued in the National Emissions Inventory, airports are the top source of lead emissions in 42 out of 50 US States based on the 2011 NEI data tables (spreadsheet summary with pivot tables attached). Because most commercial airliners burn unleaded kerosene-based jet fuel, I must conclude that the general aviation fleet of 209,034 private planes [4] is the source of this lead. We should not make policies that pander to private plane owners at the expense of children’s health. The policy assessment for the proposed rule in question identified young children as the most sensitive endpoint associated with Pb exposure. There are tens of millions of children in this country. They should not be put at risk for the gratuitous benefit, namely, private air travel, of a small minority.

 

I strongly urge you to revise the current National Ambient Air Quality Standards for lead to a level that is requisite to protect the public from the many adverse effects associated with this insidious pollutant.

 

Sincerely, [jwess]

Game 6 of the 2003 NLCS was on October 14, 2003. We all know what happened, so I'm not going to recount the happenings that horrible night, nor the eventual Game 7 loss the next night.

Since the Florida Marlins advanced to the World Series following the Cubs' collapse, they still needed use of their baseball field. At the time, they shared Joe Robbie Stadium with the Miami Dolphins (an arrangement fans of both teams felt was less than ideal. Because they still needed to use their baseball field, the dirt diamond had to remain for an extra week or two.

On October 19, 2003 the Miami Dolphins hosted the New England Patriots. Olindo Mare, the Dolphins' sure-footed (at that time) kicker, missed two game-winning kicks in the 4th quarter. Both kicks were missed because Mare slipped on the infield dirt of the Marlins' infield. New England went on to win the game in overtime. The Dolphins would end the season with a 10-6 record, missing the playoffs by one game.

The coach of the Dolphins at the time was Dave Wannstedt. Following the 2003 postseason, a second straight postseason without the Dolphins after not missing since 1996, some Dolphins left the team and the team was restructured. Pair that with a poor draft by Wannstedt and company, and 2004 started rough. With Miami's record an embarrassing 1-8, Dave Wannstedt left the team. Two months later, he became coach at Pitt.

In his third season at Pitt, Wannstedt took his team 75 miles south to play #2 West Virginia in the final game of the 2007 season. I'm not going to go into detail here, but we all know Wannstedt pulled a rabbit out of his hat and somehow vaulted that 4-7 team to a victory that night. I've never heard 60k people more silent in my life.

The loss knocked WVU out of the national title game, and knocked LSU in. LSU had been upset a week earlier by rival Arkansas, or they would've been in to begin with. The following week, WVU's head coach Rich Rodriguez left the program to coach at Michigan. LSU went on to win the national championship, in what would become the second of seven straight for the SEC.

I (along with many others) believe if WVU had won that game against Pitt, Rich Rodriguez would not have left WVU. What coach would leave right before coaching his alma mater in what could've been their first national title? If Rodriguez wouldn't have taken the job, many believe Michigan would've gotten Les Miles to take over. It would've been easier to pry him away after a disappointing loss against their rival and a "routine" Sugar Bowl appearance.

So, the national championship would've either gone to the Big East (WVU) or Big Ten (Ohio State) that night, and LSU may have been forced to reload their staff that offseason. SEC schools couldn't have used their" X-straight titles" angle for 2008 and forward. LSU has been involved in many important SEC games since then. Who knows how they might have turned out, and how that would've affected the end-of-season #1 and #2 from 2008 til now.

Adding a successful coach like Les Miles to the B1G would have kept them more relevant during the period that became the SEC's stranglehold on college football (God bless you FSU for ending it). LSU had a real chance of slipping back into irrelevancy like they were for the entire decade of the 90's. Taking another power program away from the SEC loosens their death grip even more.

So therefore, the blame for the dark period in college football from 2007-2013 lies squarely on the shoulders of WVU and Steve Bartman.
